title: Judging a life story

arm_blocks.content:
Please, read the following text carefully. We will ask you questions about it:
Peter is a philosophy professor who is passionate about philosophy. He devotes his life to teaching philosophy and transmitting his love of his discipline. Overall, the various events that occur in his life are stable and predictable, allowing him to make sense of his life and giving him the impression that the world is understandable. His surrounding makes him feel that his life is significant and full of value. He works hard, has a wife and two kids. He lives peacefully, working and spending time with his family until his death at age 75.
After his death, none of his former students remember his teaching because at the time they were not interested nor captivated by its lessons.

arm_blocks.question: He had a positive impact on people around his.
He has made a positive contribution to society in his own way.
His existence positively affected people he met.
He made a difference in a positive way.
His life as a whole had meaning.
His entire existence was full of meaning.
His life was meaningless.
His existence was empty of meaning.
Most things that happened in his life made sense.
By and large, he was able to understand the world around his.
He could comprehend what his life was all about.
He could easily make sense of his life.
He has pursued one or more big purposes in his life.
He was highly committed to certain core goals in his life.
He had a set of core goals that gave his life a sense of direction.
His daily activities were consistent with a broader life purpose.
His life was full of value.
His personal existence was significant.
Every day he experienced the sense that life was worth living.
He was not a morally good person.
He had a good moral character.
To which extent was Peter's life meaningful?
To which extent was Peter's life happy?
To which extent was Peter's life enviable?
To which extent did Peter perceive his own life as meaningful?

Please, read the following text carefully. We will ask you questions about it:
Alexandra is a scientist who devotes her life to finding cures for deadly diseases. What happens in her life is stable and predictable, giving her the feeling that she can easily make sense of her past and present. Those who surround her make her feel that her life has value and is worth living. She works hard, has a husband and two kids. At age 35, she discovers a drug that cures a painful disease and is praised by the world until her death at age 75.

After her death, it was discovered that the drug caused severe birth defects in babies conceived by people taking the drug. It is known that this was unintentional, that she conducted several scientific studies to ensure the safety of the drug, and that Alexandra truly believed that the drug would cure the disease. Her drug is said to have caused more harm than good and Alexandra's work is discredited.

consent_sections: FOR QUESTIONS ABOUT THE STUDY, CONTACT:
Noah Goodman, PhD, Department of Psychology, Stanford University, Building 420, 450 Jane Stanford Way, Stanford, CA 94305. Phone: (650) 725-2400.

You are invited to participate in a research study about how well automated computer tools can summarise published psychology studies. You will be asked to read a short story about a person's life and answer one question about it. There are no right or wrong answers and we are interested in your own view.

The purpose of this research is to check how accurately automated computer tools can summarise published psychology studies. We are re-asking questions taken from a previously published study so that we can compare the answers with the original study's results.
You must be 18 or older to take part in this study.
Participation in this research is voluntary, and you are free to withdraw your consent at any time.
Your participation will take approximately 5 minutes.
You will receive $0.96, paid through Prolific, as payment for your participation.
The risks associated with this study are minimal. The greatest risk is a breach of confidentiality, and it is small because we hold nothing that identifies you.

Your answers will be kept confidential. We do not collect your name, your email address, or your IP address. Your answers are stored with your Prolific ID only, which we use to pay you and to avoid duplicate submissions; Stanford cannot use it to find out who you are. We have procedures to protect your privacy, and your identity will not be included in written materials resulting from the study.
Questions: If you have any questions, concerns or complaints about this research, its procedures, risks and benefits, contact the Protocol Director, Noah Goodman, at (650) 725-2400.

INDEPENDENT CONTACT: If you are not satisfied with how this study is being conducted, or if you have any concerns, complaints, or general questions about the research or your rights as a participant, contact the Stanford Institutional Review Board (IRB) to speak to someone independent of the research team at 650-723-5244 or toll free at 1-866-680-2906. You can also write to the Stanford IRB at irbeducation@stanford.edu.
Save or print a copy of this page for your records.
If you agree to participate in this research, click the Continue button below.
